Question 3 of 11 · Is there a Creator?

Does the universe need a cause?

If the universe began, what could explain its beginning? Quantum physics, infinite chains and simulations, examined one by one.

The case

01

Does everything that begins to exist have a cause?

Has anything ever come into existence from absolutely nothing, with no cause whatsoever?

02

So — the universe began, and everything that begins has a cause. What caused the universe?

The cause must exist outside space, time, matter and energy — since it created all of those.

What must this cause be like?

The cause must be: outside of time (eternal), outside of space (non-physical), enormously powerful, and must have a will — since it chose to create at a specific moment.

Read more

This is what philosophers call a 'Necessary Being' — something that exists by necessity. All major philosophical traditions converge on this description.

Objections, answered

The strongest pushback we hear, and our answer to each.

You might say“No — quantum physics shows things can appear from nothing”

Our answer

Quantum events still have causes.

What quantum physics actually says

Virtual particles don't appear from 'nothing' — they appear from a quantum vacuum, a sea of energy governed by physical laws. Nothing means: no space, no time, no energy, no laws.

Even physicist Lawrence Krauss, who wrote 'A Universe from Nothing', was challenged by scientists who pointed out his 'nothing' still contained quantum fields — which is something.

ArticleDavid Albert's critique — NY Times↗(opens in a new tab)
You might say“Maybe the universe caused itself”

Our answer

Can something cause itself?

The logical problem

For the universe to cause itself, it would have to exist before it existed — a logical contradiction. A thing cannot act before it is.

You might say“Maybe it was an infinite chain of causes”

Our answer

An infinite chain of causes doesn't work.

Why infinite regress fails

An infinite regress never explains anything — it postpones the question forever. Think of it like a train: if there's no engine, no number of carriages can move.

We now know time itself began with the universe. So an infinite past chain of causes is physically impossible — there was no 'before' the universe.

You might say“Maybe it's all a simulation”

Our answer

A simulation still needs a simulator.

The simulation doesn't escape the question

Even if our universe is a simulation, something had to run it. That simulator exists outside our space, time, and matter — and chose to create our universe at a specific moment. That's exactly the description of what we call a Creator.

Read more

The simulation hypothesis, popularized by philosopher Nick Bostrom, doesn't solve the problem of first cause — it pushes it one level up. Whatever runs the simulation must itself exist, have power to create, and have made a choice. Those attributes map directly onto what every major religion has called God.

You can keep asking 'who simulated the simulator?' — but at some point, there must be a first, uncaused cause. Something that exists by its own nature, with no need for a prior cause. That's the very definition of God.

You might say“We just don't know”

Our answer

'We don't know' is honest — but let's follow the evidence.

From 'we don't know' to 'we can reason'

'We don't know' is different from 'there is no answer.' The evidence points strongly toward a cause that is timeless, spaceless, and enormously powerful — matching what every major tradition calls God.
